:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Express $\cos\left( x - \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right)$ in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\cos(u - v) = \cos u \cos v + \sin u \sin v
$$

Applying the difference formula for cosine with $u = x$ and $v = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(x-\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot 0+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot 1 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Simplify $\cos(t-\pi)$ in terms of $\sin t$ or $\cos t$.

Use the difference formula

$$
\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v
$$

and the exact values $\cos\pi=-1$ and $\sin\pi=0$.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Apply the difference formula with $u=t$ and $v=\pi$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos(t-\pi)&=\cos t\cos\pi+\sin t\sin\pi\\
&=\cos t\cdot(-1)+\sin t\cdot0\\
&=-\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The sine term vanishes; the cosine term changes sign.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Express $\cos\left(t-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ in terms of $\sin t$ and $\cos t$. Enter the signed coefficients.

$\cos\left(t-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=$ {{field-1}} $\sin t\,+$ {{field-2}} $\cos t$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Use the difference formula:

$$
\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.
$$

The angle $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ lies in quadrant II with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$, so

$$
\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\qquad \sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac12.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos\left(t-\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)&=\cos t\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}+\sin t\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\\
&=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos t+\frac12\sin t\\
&=\frac12\sin t+\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

In the requested sine-then-cosine order, the coefficients are $\frac12$ and $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. The plus sign between the fields does not remove the negative sign from the second coefficient.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Express $\cos\left(t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ in terms of $\sin t$ or $\cos t$.

$\cos\left(t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=$ {{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The sum formula has a minus sign between the products:

$$
\cos(u+v)=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v.
$$

Substitute $u=t$ and $v=\frac{\pi}{2}$, using $\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0$ and $\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos\left(t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&=\cos t\cos\frac{\pi}{2}-\sin t\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\\
&=\cos t\cdot0-\sin t\cdot1\\
&=-\sin t.
\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Express $\cos\left(x+\pi\right)$ in terms of $\sin x$ or $\cos x$.

$\cos\left(x+\pi\right)=$ {{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Use the sum formula:

$$
\cos(u+v)=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v
$$

With $u=x$ and $v=\pi$, the exact values are $\cos(\pi)=-1$ and $\sin(\pi)=0$. Substitute and collect the terms in the requested order:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos\left(x+\pi\right)&=\cos x\cos\left(\pi\right)-\sin x\sin\left(\pi\right)\\
&=\cos x\cdot\left(-1\right)-\sin x\cdot\left(0\right)\\
&=-\cos x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the difference formula:

$$
\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v
$$

With $u=\theta$ and $v=2\pi$, the exact values are $\cos(2\pi)=1$ and $\sin(2\pi)=0$. Substitute and collect the terms in the requested order:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos\left(\theta-2\pi\right)&=\cos \theta\cos\left(2\pi\right)+\sin \theta\sin\left(2\pi\right)\\
&=\cos \theta\cdot\left(1\right)+\sin \theta\cdot\left(0\right)\\
&=\cos \theta.
\end{aligned}
$$
